Notes: 1 Maccabees 15:15-23: the Roman consul Lucius (identified as L. Calpurnius Piso, cos. 139 BCE; chronology debated) writes on behalf of the Jews, after the embassy of the high priest Simon, "to Delos" among other states, telling them not to harm the Jews. Conventionally c. 139 BCE (c.). Traditionally taken as the earliest literary reference to Jews on Delos; Matassa (2018) warns that the letter itself does not mention Jews living on Delos, so as evidence of residents it is indirect. No size. [Review fix: Year Established changed from -213 to -139: first Jewish (not Samaritan) evidence: the Roman letter to Delos on behalf of the Jews, 1 Macc 15:23, c. 139 BCE; the earlier "Israelites" inscriptions are Samaritan]

Bruneau & Bordreuil, "Les Israélites de Délos et la juiverie délienne" (BCH 106, 1982), opening paragraph: "On a toujours su qu'existait à Délos, dès la seconde moitié du IIe siècle, une colonie juive", and two Jewish imprecations are among the earliest-known Delian inscriptions. Second half of 2nd c. BCE = midpoint -125 (c.). Indicates an established Jewish colony; no size given.

Inscription ID 2330, found in building GD 80: "Laodike to God Most High (Theos Hypsistos), for healing ... an offering", dated c. 108/107 BCE. Plassart, Bruneau and Trümper treat the Theos Hypsistos dedications in GD 80 as Jewish (or Samaritan) and thus as evidence of a Jewish place of worship; Matassa argues the text is a Greek votive possibly from the cult of Zeus Hypsistos and that the Jewish attribution is unproven. Disputed evidence of presence; no size.

Two near-identical funerary imprecations (SIG 1181 = I.Délos 2532) found on Rheneia, the burial island of Delos, c. 100 BCE (c.): prayers to "God the Most High" to avenge the murder (by treachery or poison) of two young women, Heraclea and Marthine. The source calls the appeal to God the Most High clearly Jewish (translation from P. van der Horst, Ancient Jewish Epitaphs, p. 149). Two named Jewish individuals of the Delos community; indicates Jewish families resident and burying their dead on Rheneia.

Monika Trümper, Hesperia 73 (2004) 513-598, abstract: five construction phases of the Delos "synagogue" (GD 80) are distinguished, "two predate 88 B.C."; its features (large hall, water reservoir, eastern orientation, isolated seashore location) "confirm its function as a synagogue from the earliest phase onward". Year = c. pre-88 BCE phases (c. 100 BCE, approximate). If accepted, the oldest known Diaspora synagogue building and evidence of an organised community; the identification is disputed (Mazur 1935, Matassa 2007/2018). No size.

EVENT: during the First Mithridatic War Delos was raided by Menophanes, general of Mithridates VI; according to Pausanias (3.23.2) and Appian (Mithr. 28) some 20,000 of the island's inhabitants were slaughtered (ancient figure for all inhabitants, not Jews; a death toll, so not a population). Matassa reports Bruneau's view that the endurance of the Jewish cult on Delos "even after the destructions of 88 BCE and 69 BCE" confirms the literary sources, i.e. the community survived. Binder suggests GD 80 was damaged in 88 or 69 BCE and then turned into (or repaired as) a synagogue.

EVENT: further destruction of Delos by the pirate Athenodoros during the Third Mithridatic War (74-63 BCE); in 69 BCE Gaius Triarius, legate of Lucullus, repaired some damage and walled the town centre. Matassa dates the adaptation of GD 80 with benches (re-using marble from the gymnasium plundered in the pirate raids) to after 74-63 BCE. By the mid-1st c. BCE Delos was in commercial decline. No figures for Jews.

Josephus, Antiquities 14.231-232, "Decree of the Delians" (archon Boiotos, 20 Thargelion): the legate M. Piso, levying troops, ordered that Jews who are Roman citizens not be harassed about military service because the consul L. Cornelius Lentulus had exempted the Jews. Eilers dates it to 49 BCE (some prefer 48) but argues it is not a decree and "cannot come from Delos" (Delos was then an Athenian cleruchy and the archon is not an Athenian/Delian one); Josephus probably added the title in error. As presented by Josephus it would imply Jewish Roman citizens on Delos; Eilers rejects the attribution. No size.

Josephus, Antiquities 14.213-216 (14.10.8): letter of "Julius Gaius" to the magistrates, council and people of Parium (or Paros): "The Jews in Delos and some of the neighbouring Jews ... have appealed to me" because a statute prevented them from observing their customs, collecting contributions and holding common meals; Roman official orders the restriction revoked. Dated c. 44 BCE by the source (Matassa: middle of 1st c. BCE). Matassa calls it the only clear and plausible literary reference to Jews resident on Delos. Shows an organised Jewish community holding communal meals and collecting funds; no size.

According to this summary the excavator (Plassart/Bruneau) concluded that the GD 80 synagogue "was in use from the First Century BC into the Second Century AD", and Trümper distinguishes phases of occupation from the 2nd c. BCE to the 2nd c. CE; the assembly hall was divided into two rooms probably after 88 BCE. 1st c. CE = midpoint 50 (c.). Indicates (if the identification is accepted) continued Jewish/Samaritan communal presence on a declining island into the 1st c. CE; no size. Secondary popular summary; identification contested by Matassa.
